introduction-the-problem-of-secret-spraw.core: Secret sprawl is credentials (DB passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates) scattered across code, config files, CI variables, wikis and chat, each copy a leak waiting to happen and impossible to rotate. Leaked secrets are among the most common breach causes. A secrets management system centralises storage, encrypts at rest, controls and audits access by identity, and enables rotation, or better, short-lived dynamic credentials that expire on their own.

first_principles.problem: A DB password committed to Git five years ago is still valid, used by 30 services, and nobody dares rotate it.
truths: Every copy is a leak risk.

analogy.title: Spare house keys under every doormat in town
analogy.story: Convenient for everyone, but you can never change the lock without hunting them all down.
analogy.breaks: House keys are physical and countable; digital secrets copy invisibly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Live leaked keys are found and revoked.

code.text:
gitleaks detect --source . --log-opts="--all"   # scans full history
trufflehog git file://. --only-verified        # checks if keys are live
# remediation: revoke first, then rewrite history

check.q: After finding a secret in Git history, what's the first step?
check.a: Revoke or rotate it; deleting it from history doesn't undo the exposure.

the-gold-standard-hashicorp-vault-archit.core: HashiCorp Vault is a central secrets broker. Clients authenticate (auth methods), receive a token bound to policies, and use it to read or generate secrets through secrets engines. All data is encrypted by a barrier key before hitting the storage backend (Raft integrated storage), and every request is audit-logged. Vault runs as an HA cluster with one active node; it starts sealed and must be unsealed before it can decrypt anything.

first_principles.problem: Each team runs its own ad-hoc secret store with different access rules, and no single audit trail exists.
truths: Access should be identity- and policy-based.

analogy.title: A bank with a vault, tellers and a ledger
analogy.story: You prove who you are at the counter, the teller checks what you're allowed, fetches from the vault, and every withdrawal is written down.
analogy.breaks: Banks store cash; Vault can also mint new credentials on demand.

check.q: What does the Vault barrier do?
check.a: It encrypts all data before it reaches the storage backend, so storage alone reveals nothing.

vault-the-seal-and-the-keys-to-the-kingd.core: Vault's data is encrypted with an encryption key, which is itself encrypted by a root key. When Vault starts it is sealed, meaning it knows where data is but can't decrypt it. Unsealing reconstructs the root key: with Shamir's Secret Sharing, a quorum of key holders (such as 3 of 5) submit shares; with auto-unseal, a cloud KMS or HSM decrypts the root key. Sealing on demand is an emergency brake, and no single person ever holds the whole key.

first_principles.problem: A single admin holds the only master key, which creates both a bus-factor risk and an insider-threat risk.
truths: No single person should hold all power.
derivation: Split the root key with **Shamir (k of n)**.

analogy.title: A nuclear launch requiring two keys turned at once
analogy.story: No individual can act alone; a quorum is needed to unlock the power.
analogy.breaks: Launch keys are physical; auto-unseal shifts the trust to a cloud KMS key.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Unsealing requires a quorum or a protected KMS key.

code.text:
vault operator init -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3
vault operator unseal   # run by 3 different holders

# or in config:
# seal "awskms" { kms_key_id = "alias/vault-unseal" }

check.a: It removes human toil, but whoever controls the KMS key effectively controls Vault's unsealing.

vault-getting-in-auth-methods.core: Auth methods let clients prove identity to Vault and receive a scoped, expiring token, ideally using identity the platform already provides so there's no 'secret zero' to distribute. Kubernetes auth verifies a pod's service-account JWT, AWS/GCP auth verifies signed cloud identity documents, AppRole uses a role ID plus a wrapped secret ID, OIDC/LDAP serve humans, and JWT auth lets CI systems like GitHub Actions log in with their OIDC tokens.

first_principles.problem: To fetch secrets, every app needs a Vault token, so teams bake a long-lived token into config, recreating the original problem.

analogy.title: Entering an office with your company badge
analogy.story: Building security trusts the badge office's issuance instead of handing out a separate password to every visitor.
analogy.breaks: Badges are long-lived; good Vault tokens expire within minutes or hours.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Pods get Vault tokens using identity they already have.

code.text:
vault auth enable kubernetes
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/orders \
  bound_service_account_names=orders \
  bound_service_account_namespaces=prod \
  policies=orders-app ttl=1h
# pod logs in with its SA JWT; no stored secret

check.a: Needing an initial secret to fetch secrets; platform identity auth methods solve it.

vault-engines-static-vs-dynamic-secrets.core: Secrets engines are Vault plugins that store or generate secrets. Static engines (KV v2) store values with versioning, which you rotate yourself. Dynamic engines (database, AWS, PKI) generate unique credentials on request with a lease: each app instance gets its own DB user that Vault revokes when the lease expires. Dynamic secrets shrink exposure windows, give per-consumer attribution, and make leaked credentials expire on their own. The transit engine provides encryption as a service without exposing keys.

first_principles.problem: All 50 instances share one DB password; when it leaks, you can't tell which instance leaked it, and rotating breaks everything.
truths: Shared static creds can't be attributed.
derivation: Use **KV v2** for unavoidable static secrets.
Use **database engine** for per-app DB users.
Use **AWS engine** for temp IAM creds.

analogy.title: Hotel key cards versus a shared house key
analogy.story: Each guest gets their own card that stops working at checkout, while a house key copied to everyone works forever.
analogy.breaks: Hotels reprogram cards manually; Vault creates and revokes users in the database automatically.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each instance gets a unique, expiring DB user.

code.text:
vault write database/roles/orders-ro db_name=pg \
  creation_statements="CREATE ROLE \"{{name}}\" LOGIN PASSWORD '{{password}}' VALID UNTIL '{{expiration}}'; GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO \"{{name}}\";" \
  default_ttl=1h max_ttl=24h
vault read database/creds/orders-ro
# username v-k8s-orders-ro-7Xq... lease_duration 1h

check.q: Why are dynamic secrets better for incident response?
check.a: Each credential is unique, so a leak identifies its source and can be revoked without affecting others.

the-cloud-native-way-aws-secrets-manager.core: AWS Secrets Manager is a managed secrets store integrated with IAM, KMS and AWS services. Secrets are encrypted with KMS keys, access is controlled by IAM and resource policies, every access is logged in CloudTrail, and Lambda-based rotation can change RDS passwords on a schedule. It trades Vault's flexibility (dynamic engines, multi-cloud) for zero operations within AWS. SSM Parameter Store is a cheaper option for simpler config.

first_principles.problem: A small AWS-only team needs rotation and auditing but can't operate an HA Vault cluster.
derivation: Store in **Secrets Manager** with a **KMS CMK**.

analogy.title: A building's managed safe-deposit service
analogy.story: You don't build or guard the vault; the building does, and your badge already opens your box.
analogy.breaks: It's tied to one building (AWS); multi-cloud needs something else.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No stored keys; rotation is transparent.

code.text:
import boto3, json
sm = boto3.client("secretsmanager")      # creds from the task/instance role
secret = json.loads(sm.get_secret_value(SecretId="prod/orders/db")["SecretString"])
# rotation updates AWSCURRENT; cache with a short TTL

check.q: Why cache secrets client-side with a TTL?
check.a: To cut API cost and latency while still picking up rotated values reasonably quickly.

secrets-in-kubernetes-external-secrets-o.core: Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded and, by default, stored unencrypted in etcd, and storing them in Git is unsafe. The External Secrets Operator (ESO) keeps the source of truth in an external manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP, Azure). An ExternalSecret resource declares what to fetch, and ESO syncs it into a native Secret on a refresh interval, so GitOps manifests contain only references, not values. Pair it with etcd encryption at rest and tight RBAC on Secrets.

first_principles.problem: Teams commit base64 Kubernetes Secret YAML to Git, believing it's encrypted.
truths: Git should hold references, not values.

analogy.title: A menu that names dishes while the recipes stay locked in the kitchen
analogy.story: The menu (Git) says what's needed; the kitchen (secret manager) holds the real recipe.
analogy.breaks: Once plated, the dish is on the table: synced Secrets still live in etcd, so protect them.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Git holds only the reference; the value syncs at runtime.

check.q: Does ESO remove the need for etcd encryption?
check.a: No. Synced Secrets still live in etcd, so encryption at rest and RBAC remain necessary.

the-root-of-trust-hsms-hardware-security.core: A Hardware Security Module (HSM) is tamper-resistant hardware that generates and stores keys and performs crypto operations inside itself, so private keys never leave in plaintext. It's the root of trust for CAs, payment PINs, code signing and Vault auto-unseal. HSMs are certified (FIPS 140-2/3 Level 3), detect tampering and zeroise keys, and are accessed via PKCS#11. Cloud KMS services are multi-tenant HSM-backed APIs, while CloudHSM gives single-tenant devices.

first_principles.problem: A CA's root signing key sits in a file on a server; one compromise lets attackers mint trusted certificates for any domain.
truths: Keys in software can be copied.
Some keys are catastrophic to lose.

analogy.title: A sealed notary machine that stamps documents but never gives up its seal
analogy.story: You feed it papers and get them stamped; the seal itself can't be removed without destroying the machine.
analogy.breaks: An HSM can't stop misuse by authorised callers; access control around it still matters.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Signatures without any exportable private key.

code.text:
aws kms create-key --key-spec ECC_NIST_P256 --key-usage SIGN_VERIFY
aws kms sign --key-id alias/release-signing \
  --message fileb://digest.bin --message-type DIGEST \
  --signing-algorithm ECDSA_SHA_256
# the private key never leaves the HSM fleet

check.q: Does an HSM prevent an attacker who has app credentials from signing malware?
check.a: No. It prevents key theft, not misuse; authorisation, approvals and monitoring are still needed.
